Objective\n35\t\n36\t> **A static website that accepts a file from the user and turns it into a visual\n37\t> transmission on screen, which a second device running the same page receives through\n38\t> its camera and reconstructs into the original file.**\n39\t>\n40\t> **It must handle large files — on the order of multiple gigabytes.**\n41\t\n42\t- **Static.** No backend. The\n51\tdesign must never *forbid* a large file, run out of memory, or blow up super-linearly.\n52\tBut the channel's physics are what they are:\n53\t\n54\t| File size | Stage 1 (30 KB/s) | Stage 2 (60 KB/s) | Stage 3 (106 KB/s) |\n55\t|---|---|---|---|\n56\t| 100 MB | 57 min | 28 min | 16 min |\n57\t| **1 GB** | **9.7 h** | **4.9 h** | **2.7 h** |\n58\t| **10 GB** | **4.0 days** | **2.0 days** | **27.5 h** |\n59\t| 100 GB | 40.5 days | 20.2 days | 11.4 days |\n60\t| 1 TB | 414 days | 207 days | 117 days |\n61\t\n62\t> All figures are **user-visible file bytes**, not wire bytes. See §13.2 — with\n63\t> compression on, the two differ by 3–10× on compressible input, and quoting the wrong\n64\t> one would overstate throughput.\n65\t\n66\t**Gigabytes are hours-to-days. Terabytes are months.** Three design consequences follow,\n67\tand they are as load-bearing as any coding decision:\n68\t\n69\t1. **Resume is not optional** (D22). Nobody holds a phone for 27 hours.\n70\t2. **Neither side may hold the file in memory** (D20).\n71\t3. **The app states the estimated time before the user commits** (D23). Letting someone\n72\t   start a 40-day transfer without saying so is a product failure, not an edge case.\n73\t\n74\t---\n75\t\n76\t## 2. Glossary\n77\t\n78\tSeveral of these words are overloaded in the surrounding literature, and two of them\n79\t(*block*, *frame*) mean different things in different research documents. Within this\n80\tplan they mean exactly this:\n81\t\n82\t| Term | Meaning here |\n83\t|---|---|\n84\t| **Fragment** | The atomic unit the fountain code operates over. Fixed length **L** for the whole session (D15). |\n85\t| **K** | Number of fragments in one block. Derived as `blockSize / L`; never transmitted (D7). |\n86\t| **Block** | A contiguous slice of the (possibly compressed) payload, cut into K fragments and fountain-coded independently. **Always means this** — never \"fountain block\" or \"QR block\". |\n87\t| **Packet** | One fountain-coded symbol: 13-byte header + L payload bytes. The unit a tile carries. |\n88\t| **Tile** | One QR symbol on screen. Carries exactly one packet. |\n89\t| **Frame** | One displayed image, containing a grid of tiles. **Never** a video frame — those are *camera frames*. |\n90\t| **Camera frame** | One image captured by the receiver's camera. |\n91\t| **Beacon** | A special **packet** carrying file-level metadata instead of payload. Beacon packets are encoded into tiles and mixed into display frames by the frame mixer (D17, §7.2). |\n92\t| **Profile** | A modulation configuration: QR version, module pixel size, tile count. Several coexist per frame (D16). |\n93\t| **Dwell** | How many packets the sender emits for one block before advancing (§8.1). |\n94\t| **Screen px** | A pixel on the *sender's display*. What the renderer controls. |\n95\t| **Camera px** | A pixel in the *receiver's captured frame*. What the decoder actually sees. |\n96\t| **px/module** | **Always CAMERA px per module unless explicitly written \"screen px/module\".** The 4 px/module decode cliff is a *camera*-pixel figure. Conflating the two put every S2/S3 optical run below the cliff — see `../notes/spike-results.md` §S3. |\n97\t| **Magnification** | `camera_px_per_module = screen_px_per_module × M`, where `M` = (capture width across the code region) / (code region width in screen px). A 1920-px-wide landscape code region filling a 1080-px-wide portrait capture gives **M = 0.5625**, so 4 screen px/module is only **2.25 camera px/module**. |\n98\t| **Erasure** | A packet that did not arrive or failed validation. Everything else is explanation.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Objective\n\n> **A static website that accepts a file from the user and turns it into a visual\n> transmission on screen, which a second device running the same page receives through\n> its camera and reconstructs into the original file.**\n>\n> **It must handle large files — on the order of multiple gigabytes.**\n\n- **Static.** No backend. Files on a CDN, works offline, auditable once and trusted\n  thereafter. There is nowhere to upload anything *to*.\n- **Same page, both roles.** One deployment; the user picks sender or receiver.\n- **Screen → camera is the only channel.** Strictly one-way, lossy, low-bandwidth.\n- **Multi-gigabyte.** The requirement that most shapes the architecture (§3).\n\n### 1.1 The honest framing of \"multiple gigabytes\"\n\nMulti-GB support is an **architectural** requirement, not a performance promise. The\ndesign must never *forbid* a large file, run out of memory, or blow up super-linearly.\nBut the channel's physics are what they are:\n\n| File size | Stage 1 (30 KB/s) | Stage 2 (60 KB/s) | Stage 3 (106 KB/s) |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| 100 MB | 57 min | 28 min | 16 min |\n| **1 GB** | **9.7 h** | **4.9 h** | **2.7 h** |\n| **10 GB** | **4.0 days** | **2.0 days** | **27.5 h** |\n| 100 GB | 40.5 days | 20.2 days | 11.4 days |\n| 1 TB | 414 days | 207 days | 117 days |\n\n> All figures are **user-visible file bytes**, not wire bytes. See §13.2 — with\n> compression on, the two differ by 3–10× on compressible input, and quoting the wrong\n> one would overstate throughput.\n\n**Gigabytes are hours-to-days. Terabytes are months.** Three design consequences follow,\nand they are as load-bearing as any coding decision:\n\n1. **Resume is not optional** (D22). Nobody holds a phone for 27 hours.\n2. **Neither side may hold the file in memory** (D20).\n3. **The app states the estimated time before the user commits** (D23). Letting someone\n   start a 40-day transfer without saying so is a product failure, not an edge case.\n\n---\n\n## 2. Glossary\n\nSeveral of these words are overloaded in the surrounding literature, and two of them\n(*block*, *frame*) mean different things in different research documents. Within this\nplan they mean exactly this:\n\n| Term | Meaning here |\n|---|---|\n| **Fragment** | The atomic unit the fountain code operates over. Fixed length **L** for the whole session (D15). |\n| **K** | Number of fragments in one block. Derived as `blockSize / L`; never transmitted (D7). |\n| **Block** | A contiguous slice of the (possibly compressed) payload, cut into K fragments and fountain-coded independently. **Always means this** — never \"fountain block\" or \"QR block\". |\n| **Packet** | One fountain-coded symbol: 13-byte header + L payload bytes. The unit a tile carries. |\n| **Tile** | One QR symbol on screen. Carries exactly one packet. |\n| **Frame** | One displayed image, containing a grid of tiles. **Never** a video frame — those are *camera frames*. |\n| **Camera frame** | One image captured by the receiver's camera. |\n| **Beacon** | A special **packet** carrying file-level metadata instead of payload. Beacon packets are encoded into tiles and mixed into display frames by the frame mixer (D17, §7.2). |\n| **Profile** | A modulation configuration: QR version, module pixel size, tile count. Several coexist per frame (D16). |\n| **Dwell** | How many packets the sender emits for one block before advancing (§8.1). |\n| **Screen px** | A pixel on the *sender's display*. What the renderer controls. |\n| **Camera px** | A pixel in the *receiver's captured frame*. What the decoder actually sees. |\n| **px/module** | **Always CAMERA px per module unless explicitly written \"screen px/module\".** The 4 px/module decode cliff is a *camera*-pixel figure. Conflating the two put every S2/S3 optical run below the cliff — see `../notes/spike-results.md` §S3. |\n| **Magnification** | `camera_px_per_module = screen_px_per_module × M`, where `M` = (capture width across the code region) / (code region width in screen px). A 1920-px-wide landscape code region filling a 1080-px-wide portrait capture gives **M = 0.5625**, so 4 screen px/module is only **2.25 camera px/module**. |\n| **Erasure** | A packet that did not arrive or failed validation. Never a corrupted packet — those are discarded, not used. |\n| **Stage** | A modulation generation: 1 = tiled mono QR, 2 = + RGB tripling, 3 = custom grid codec. |\n| **Pass** | One complete traversal of every block by the sender. |","numLines":100,"startLine":1,"totalLines":1596}}}
